questions.prompt: Six strawberries are on a plate. You eat two. How many remain?
questions.explanation: Remove one to leave five, then another to leave four.

questions.prompt: You start with 3 counters and take away all 3. How many remain?
questions.explanation: Every counter has been removed. None remain, and we write that as zero.

questions.prompt: Which check shows that 6 − 2 = 4 makes sense?
questions.explanation: Put the two removed counters back with the four remaining ones. You return to six.

title: Subtraction explained: where did the strawberries go?
practice: Try a few calculations in Math Rush, or take your time with the examples above.

sections.html:
Subtraction finds the difference between two amounts. One way to picture it is taking something away: start with 6 strawberries, eat 2, and 4 remain.

That is 6 − 2 = 4. The strawberries have had a short but useful career in maths.

If counting feels new, start with putting small groups together.
sections.title: What does subtraction mean?

sections.html:
Draw six circles for the strawberries. Cross out two, then count only the circles that remain: four.

The crossed-out circles show what you removed. Try five circles with one crossed out: four remain again, but you started with a different amount.
sections.title: See what is left

sections.html:
Read 6 − 2 = 4 as “six minus two equals four”. The − sign means minus; the answer, 4, is the difference.

Keep the order: six is the starting amount, two is what you take away.
sections.title: Read the minus sign

sections.html:
Imagine returning the two eaten strawberries to the four on the plate. You have six again: 4 + 2 = 6.

Adding back what you took away checks the subtraction. OpenStax explains this link between addition and subtraction.
sections.title: Put them back to check

sections.html:
Take all 3 counters away: 3 − 3 = 0. Take none away: 3 − 0 = 3. Same starting pile, very different endings.

These examples only remove counters you already have. Negative numbers let us describe other situations, such as owing money.

Next, try counting equal groups, or browse the basic arithmetic guide.
sections.title: What if nothing is left?

description: Six strawberries, two eaten: four left. See how subtraction works, what the minus sign means and how adding back checks your answer.
